segs.cue: you've already introduced yourself; start straight on the cover

segs.t: So my project is called Poise. It helps you notice when your posture drifts, without breaking your focus. I made a web app and a light bar that sits on your monitor.

I picked this project for two reasons. First, it shows the whole process, research, design, testing and iteration, so you can see what problem I was solving at each step. Second, I used AI all the way through, so I can show you why I used it, how I used it, and how it helped me make decisions.
So, let me walk you through how it came together.
First, the problem and my research. Then version one, what I changed, and version two. And last, what I learned using AI, and what's next.

segs.cue: quick: one short line per press

segs.t: This is how I define the problem in one sentence. We drift without noticing.
At first, we sit up straight.
Then sometimes, we rest our chin on our hand.
Bit by bit, we lean in closer to the screen.
Over time, the neck and lower back start to hurt.
And fixing it later can cost thousands. I've had neck and back pain myself, and I spent a lot on physical therapy and a good chair. And I wasn't the only one.

Then I wanted to see if this happens to other people too, so I looked at some research. First, the average US adult sits about six hours a day. Up to 63 percent of office workers get neck pain in a single year. And back and neck pain is the biggest health cost in the US, about 135 billion dollars.
So yeah, it's not just me. A lot of people sit all day, and it hurts.
So I ran a quick survey with fifteen people to see when they notice it, where it hurts, and what they've tried.

Three things stood out. Nine out of fifteen rarely notice their posture, or only once it starts to hurt. Fourteen out of fifteen feel pain somewhere after a long session, mostly the neck and lower back. And most of what they'd tried was stuff you do later, like stretching or a better chair. So basically, nobody had anything that catches it early.
To go deeper, I interviewed three of them. Paul, Hyunjoo and Peter.
So, Paul only notices he's slouching when his lower back starts to hurt.
Hyunjoo bought a Herman Miller chair. It helped at first, but then sitting straight for a long time was still hard for him.
And Peter sometimes leans toward the screen when he focuses. When he works somewhere quiet, a silent reminder would be helpful for him.
So from these interviews, I found an opportunity for each of them.
For Paul, I can help him notice earlier.
For Hyunjoo, I can give him short breaks to reset, so he can come back and sit well again.
And for Peter, I can give him a signal that doesn't interrupt him.

Next I looked at what's already out there. Posture apps are good at noticing your posture early, and the cue is clear. But they can interrupt your work because they buzz, or pop up on your screen. And chairs and Pilates are things people try after it already hurts.

So then I looked outside of posture tools, since I like seeing what ideas I can bring in from other services. Like when I order on DoorDash, I can see my order right on the lock screen without opening the app. Uber, Starbucks and Nike Run Club work in a similar way.

So I noticed a gap. Posture apps and tools either interrupt you, or come after it already hurts. So I saw a chance for something in between, that helps quietly while you work. And since status updates show my order on the lock screen without opening the app, I thought I could help people by showing their posture live.
So from all three, the cue had to come early, be clear, and not interrupt.
So I thought, if people get a clear cue that helps them notice early, with no interruptions, they'll catch the drift sooner and stay aligned longer.

So for the user, I wanted the app to tell you when you drift, and the light bar to change color as you move. That way you notice it right away, without stopping your work. And for the business, I'd keep the app free so people can try it first, and then offer the light bar. And seeing their posture get better over time would turn it into a daily habit.
Here's how it works in five steps.
First, you answer four questions, pick the camera or the sensor, and plug in the light bar.
Then you start working. The app checks your posture and the light stays white.
If you drift, the app shows you what changed and the light turns yellow, then red. When you sit back up, it turns green and slowly turns back to white.
When you finish your session, you see a report that shows how long you sat well.
Then you take a break with stretches or a game, and the light plays along.

segs.cue: the recording plays; press once per part

segs.t: So here's what it actually looks like. I'll go through four parts.

First, onboarding. Poise asks four questions, like how long you focus, how it should tell you when you drift, what helps you rest, and if breaks should start on their own. And your answers set up your focus mode. I came up with this from the interviews, because everyone worked differently, so setup starts from your own answers.

Next is focus mode. You can see the bar on the right fills up as you drift, and the label tells you how you moved, like leaning forward. And the light bar turns yellow, then red, and when you sit back up, it turns green and goes back to white.
I came up with this from the survey, because nine out of fifteen only noticed once it hurt, so the bar moves as soon as you drift and tells you what to fix.
Then break mode. This figure shows you each stretch, and the camera checks how closely you match it as a percent. Up top, you can switch to a reset or a small game.
I came up with this from the survey too, because a lot of people stretch to fix their posture, so I made this break mode to help them reset.
And last, settings. In this one sheet, you can change your modes, how bright the light bar glows, and the music.
I came up with this from the interviews, because each person wanted something different.
Then I put it in front of classmates. This was also a class project, so we had a three hour playtest in class on October 29th, and I mostly watched and took notes.
And watching people use it changed what I thought mattered. Ten people tried it with the cardboard light bar, about ten minutes each.
On the good side, people loved having options for a break, and being able to shut off the camera. So people liked having control.

But from the light alone, they couldn't tell how they moved. Twelve guide steps before they could even start felt like too much, and some worried what the camera collects. So slow setup, privacy, and a vague light.
And for new ideas, they wished they could just type what they want, and keep a small window open while they work. So people wanted it while they work.
So I planned the next version from two places. First, from classmates' feedback.
Clearer privacy. The camera prompt now says it never records, and offers the sensor. The trade off is, the camera is precise but feels watched, and the sensor feels private but less exact.

Then clearer cues. This is where my first hypothesis was wrong. I thought a quiet light alone was enough, but people needed to know what to fix. So now it says the move out loud when the light turns red. The trade off is, it's easier to notice, but a voice can interrupt.
And simpler and more personal, with plain names, Ask Poise, a mini window, and a four step guide. The trade off is, it's easier to start, but plain names hide some fine control.

Then from my own review. A better side panel, with a figure that moves with you. The figure is less exact, so the number stays, just smaller. One design system, one type scale, color set and spacing for every screen. It's easy to share, but edge cases need rules. And a calmer light bar, white, yellow, red and back to white, with no surprise green. It's calmer, but fixing your posture feels less rewarded.

So with that plan, I built version two. It's the same five steps, and what changed is in green. In set up, there's a clearer camera or sensor choice. In focus, it adds a figure and a mini window. When you drift, it says the move out loud too, and the light goes yellow, red, and back to white. In the report, you can hover the chart for each moment. And in the break, the same figure guides your stretches.

segs.cue: the recording plays; press once per change

segs.t: So here's what version two looks like. There are six changes, so I'll go through them quickly.

First, camera or sensor. Version two explains both up front. The camera sees your posture but never records it, and the sensor only measures distance, so it's a little less precise. I changed this after the playtest, because people worried what the camera collected, and weren't sure how the sensor was different.

Next, fewer steps. The guide went from twelve steps to four, grouped by what they cover. And changing a mode got simpler too, a short side panel with plain names instead of a long scroll of sliders. Twelve guide steps just felt like too much before even starting.

Then, easier to notice. A figure moves with you, and the card changes color as you drift. It also says the move out loud when the light turns red. And in the report, hovering the chart shows what moved at each moment. People liked the light, but wanted to see what to fix and when.

This is the mini window. You can pop Poise out into a small window that floats over your other tabs, so the figure and the timer stay in view while you work. People wanted a small window to keep open while they worked.

And this is Ask Poise, which is new in version two. You type or say what you want, like a one hour focus or breathing breaks, and Poise sets it for you. It reads plain words right on the laptop, so nothing is sent out. People struggled to find the settings, and wanted to set it up their own way.

And last, one look and feel. I came up with this from my own review. I built one design system from the light bar's colors. The brand color, the gradient background and the type all come from it, and the same figure shows up in focus and break mode. So every screen feels like one product.

Then I tested version two with Paul, Hyunjoo and Peter from the interviews, at their own desks for an hour each. And the fixes held up. One set it up without asking me anything, another just glanced at the figure and sat up, and someone kept the little window open all hour. So it helped without breaking focus.
But real days got in the way. One jumped on a call and it started talking, and another had to leave the little window just to take a break. So it got in the way of calls and breaks.
And for opportunities, they wanted it to just go quiet in meetings, and to see when they slouch the most each week. So people want it to fit their day and habits.
Then I measured it, with the same three people and the same tasks on both versions.

The one I cared about most is time aligned, the share of a one hour work session, because that's the hypothesis. It went from 85 percent to 90, so up 5 points. Everyone already sat well most of the time, so the gain is small, but all three went up, and Peter, who drifted the most, gained the most.

Time to get set up went from one twenty five to fifty two seconds, about 38 percent faster. That's less than going from twelve steps to four would suggest, so the questions and the camera setup are where I'd trim next. Time to change modes went from twenty one seconds to fifteen, about 28 percent faster. And satisfaction went from 2.7 to 4.3 out of 5, up 1.6 points.
So they stayed aligned longer, and it got easier to use.
Now I want to talk about what I learned using AI, across research, building and design, since I used it at almost every step.

In research, I had one month and wanted my time with people, so AI found academic papers and drafted my questions. But I read each paper myself, and cut questions that led people. So AI finds and drafts fast, but judging what fits is my job.

When I was building, I wanted a real app to test within days, not a mockup, so AI coded the app and the Arduino from my flow. Then I had people try each build and watched them drift. So AI writes code fast, but only people show if it feels right.

And for the design system, I needed every screen to feel like one product, so I wrote one guide for type, color and spacing for AI to follow. Then I lined up every screen, and fixed the rules instead of each screen. So when the rules are clear, AI keeps every screen consistent.
So yeah, AI made me a lot faster, but it was people who showed me what mattered.
So, what's next? Basically, Poise works around real days, and the light bar leaves the cardboard behind.

For the app, first, quiet during meetings. I'd read the calendar and hold cues while you're on a call, since calls were the biggest thing that broke at real desks. Then a weekly look back, a short summary of when you drift most, so the habit shows. That's also what keeps people coming back, so it matters for the business too. And later, a menu bar app, with your posture and time left right in the Mac menu bar, no window needed.

For the light bar, first, light that fits the room, brighter on sunny days and softer at night. Then cues that don't rely on color, pulse patterns as well as color, so people who are color blind can read it. And eventually, a printed bar with no cable, a 3D printed bar with a built in battery that clips onto a MacBook.
That's Poise. Thanks so much for listening. The live app and this deck are both at poise-lightbar.netlify.app, and I'd love to hear any questions you have.
